questions.topic: Guide status and scope of use
questions.question: Which statement about the status of the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 is correct?

options.A: It is a legally binding GMP regulation, which local authorities may use to replace their current local regulations
options.B: It is a mandatory standard, and a new sterile facility must be designed fully to it and be certified
options.C: It is neither a standard nor a GMP regulation, and whether to adopt it is the owner's decision
options.D: It applies only to new facilities, and its content may not be consulted when an existing facility is renovated or expanded

questions.explanation: The guide states explicitly that it is neither a standard nor a GMP regulation and does not replace applicable laws, codes and regulations; whether to apply it to new or existing facilities is at the discretion of the owner or operator. Treating it as a mandatory regulation is a common misunderstanding.

questions.question: According to §1.2, which of the following is NOT within the scope of this guide?

options.A: Facilities for injectable products manufactured by aseptic processing
options.B: Facilities for injectable products manufactured by terminal sterilization
options.C: Sterile products formulated from APIs derived from biopharmaceutical processes
options.D: Upstream process controls and equipment details for sterile APIs (see the ISPE API guide)

questions.explanation: The guide covers API and drug product facilities for both aseptic processing and terminal sterilization, and applies to formulations of both traditional chemical and biopharmaceutical origin; for sterile APIs it covers only the facility aspects, while upstream process controls and equipment are handled by the ISPE API guide.

questions.question: The guide notes that personnel are usually the largest potential source of contamination in the process. Which design principle follows directly from this?

options.A: Add more personnel for double checks to reduce the risk of contamination from human error
options.B: Minimize the interface between personnel and exposed product and contact surfaces
options.C: Increase the frequency of personnel patrols in the cleanroom so contamination problems are found sooner
options.D: Concentrate all personnel movement in a single corridor to allow monitoring and shorten travel distances

questions.explanation: Because personnel are the main source of particulate and microbial challenge, the guide requires minimizing the interface between personnel and exposed sterile materials, product, components and contact surfaces, and using environmental control technology (such as barriers) wherever possible. Adding personnel would increase the contamination risk.

questions.question: The quality of an injectable formulation is clearly affected by terminal sterilization. Following the design philosophy of the guide, which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Give priority to product requirements and adopt another controlled approach (such as aseptic processing)
options.B: Still use terminal sterilization, and relax the product quality specifications to suit the process
options.C: Stop developing the product, because the guide accepts only terminal sterilization processes
options.D: Use terminal sterilization, but downgrade the filling area to unclassified

questions.explanation: The guide recommends terminal sterilization wherever it is applicable; but if the product is significantly affected by that step, product requirements take priority and another controlled manufacturing approach is used. The basic layout is in any case driven by product and process requirements (CQAs lead to CPPs).

questions.question: Compared with the previous edition, which statement about the changes in environmental classification in the third edition is correct?

options.A: It retains ISPE's own Grade 5 classes, and gives a correspondence table to ISO classes only in an appendix
options.B: It replaces ISPE's own classes with dual ISO 5/Grade A designations, and adds LP/GAAS
options.C: It lists CNC and UC as formally defined environmental classifications under the harmonized scheme
options.D: It deletes the recommended layouts for RABS and isolators, keeping only example layouts of conventional cleanrooms

questions.explanation: The third edition deleted the ISPE classes and uses harmonized dual designations instead (for example, Grade 5 became ISO 5/Grade A), and added LP/GAAS in the relevant sections. CNC and UC are no longer defined in the harmonized designations because they are not regulatory terms; and the edition adds recommended layouts for RABS, isolators and BFS.

questions.question: What general expectation do regulators have about the method of sterilizing injectable products?

options.A: The two methods have equal standing and may be chosen freely according to capacity and cost
options.B: Aseptic processing is preferred because it is gentler on the product
options.C: Terminal sterilization should be used wherever the product is not affected
options.D: Terminal sterilization needs to be considered only for biological products

questions.explanation: Regulators state that injectable products should be terminally sterilized as long as the product is not harmed, and that products should be developed with this in mind from the start; alternatives such as aseptic processing are used only when this cannot be done. The choice between the two significantly affects facility planning.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four main cross-contamination routes listed in the guide?

options.A: Mix-Up
options.B: Retention
options.C: Mechanical Transfer (for example, carried in on equipment or carts)
options.D: Temperature excursion

questions.explanation: The four routes are Mix-Up, Retention, Mechanical Transfer and Airborne Transfer. A temperature excursion can affect quality, but it is not a route by which cross-contamination spreads.

questions.question: After a risk assessment, the team finds that the risk of a step can be reduced either by "engineering design" or by "adding SOPs and personnel checks". According to the guide, how should this be handled?

options.A: Consider engineering solutions first, supplemented by procedures where necessary
options.B: Write an SOP first, because a procedural change costs least and needs no equipment change
options.C: Both must be adopted together, with procedures taking priority over engineering design
options.D: The on-site operators decide according to the situation on the shift, without documentation

questions.explanation: The guide explains that risk can be mitigated by engineering, procedures or both, and states explicitly that wherever possible engineering solutions should be considered first rather than relying on procedures. This is also the QbD spirit of designing quality into the facility.

questions.question: When risk is expressed as an RPN (Risk Priority Number), which three factors is it a function of?

options.A: Severity, Cost and Detectability
options.B: Probability of Occurrence, Frequency of Audit and Detectability
options.C: Severity, Probability of Occurrence and Detectability
options.D: Severity, Probability of Occurrence and Regulatory Impact

questions.explanation: The document defines risk as the combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and its severity; when expressed as an RPN, it is a function of Severity, Probability of Occurrence and Detectability, after which mitigation and control schemes are developed.

questions.question: For aseptic processing in new or renovated facilities, the guide recommends barrier technology (isolators and RABS). What is the main reason?

options.A: It replaces reliance on individual operators' aseptic technique with engineered separation
options.B: It can fully replace environmental monitoring and gowning requirements, reducing the daily operating burden
options.C: Its initial investment is always lower than a conventional cleanroom, and it needs no additional validation
options.D: It lets different products share one open room without any segregation

questions.explanation: The guide lists three approaches of increasing separation: a conventional cleanroom, RABS and an isolator; and recommends barrier technology for new or renovated facilities because it is engineered separation that does not depend on individual aseptic operation. It cannot replace environmental monitoring, and it does not guarantee lower cost.

questions.question: Which statement about Grade D and the US FDA classification is correct?

options.A: Grade D is equivalent to ISO 8 in operation, and the FDA has the same corresponding class
options.B: Grade D is ISO 7 at rest, corresponds to the FDA Class 10,000, and the particle limits of the two are the same
options.C: Grade D applies only in the EU and has no at-rest particle limit requirement
options.D: The US FDA has no corresponding class; Grade D is ISO 8 at rest, while the FDA classes are based on in operation

questions.explanation: The guide notes that the US FDA has no class equivalent to Grade D; Grade D is ISO 8 "at rest", while the FDA classes are based on "in operation". This difference needs particular attention when designing a classification strategy for Grade D areas.

questions.question: Which description of CNC (Controlled Not Classified) is most accurate?

options.A: A formally defined regulatory class, between Grade C and Grade D
options.B: It originated in biologics facilities and denotes a space with access control that is cleaner than ordinary areas, without a formal classification claim
options.C: A space certified to ISO 14644-1 but not listed in EU Annex 1
options.D: A zone around Grade A that is environmentally monitored only at rest

questions.explanation: CNC originated in biologics facilities and refers to a space with access control that is cleaner than a general HVAC area but with no formal classification claim. It is not a regulatory term, and the third edition does not define it in the harmonized designations.

questions.question: How does the recommended classification of the background room differ between open aseptic operations carried out inside an isolator and those carried out under a UAF?

options.A: Both backgrounds must be ISO 7/Grade B, with no difference
options.B: The isolator background must be stricter, ISO 6 or higher
options.C: The UAF background can be ISO 8/Grade C, while an isolator needs ISO 7/Grade B
options.D: The isolator background can be ISO 8/Grade C; under a UAF the background is ISO 7/Grade B

questions.explanation: Exposed product and containers are maintained at ISO 5/Grade A or better under a UAF, with an ISO 7/Grade B background; the inside of an isolator is decontaminated with VHP or similar and is accessed only through alpha-beta transfer ports and glove ports with integrity testing, so for a globally usable facility the background room can be ISO 8/Grade C.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of open processing?

options.A: A closed sterilization tank after SIP
options.B: Closed material addition through an alpha-beta port
options.C: Transfer of vials that are partially stoppered or stoppered but not yet capped
options.D: A closed single-use assembly or container

questions.explanation: Open processing refers to times when product, materials or container closure surfaces are exposed to the surrounding process environment where quality may be affected, such as open filling, assembly, loading and unloading, and transfer of uncapped vials. The other three are examples of closed processing listed in the document.

questions.question: A process uses a potent compound with a potential inhalation hazard. When planning operator protection, what order of priority does the guide set?

options.A: PPE as the main protection, with engineering controls provided or not depending on the budget
options.B: Perform a risk analysis first and prefer engineering controls, with PPE only for leaks or as secondary protection
options.C: As soon as a hazard is identified the process must be stopped, with no risk analysis needed
options.D: Hazard and risk mean the same thing, so simply require all staff to wear PPE

questions.explanation: The guide stresses distinguishing hazard from risk, doing a risk analysis first and setting up an operator protection plan; engineering approaches take priority because they remove people from the hazard, and PPE is used only for breach situations or as a secondary measure.

questions.topic: Filling background for terminally sterilized product
questions.question: What is the "minimum" background environment for the filling of terminally sterilized products?

options.A: ISO 8/Grade C
options.B: ISO 5/Grade A
options.C: ISO 7/Grade B
options.D: Unclassified, with access control only

questions.explanation: Terminally sterilized products do not need the same environmental controls as aseptic processing, but the filling background is at least ISO 8/Grade C, often combined with component sterilization and depyrogenation, solution filtration, and LP/GAAS at the filling point to reduce bioburden and endotoxin risk.
questions.reference: ISPE Vol.3 §3.2 (Terminally Sterilized Products intro), Table 2.3 Note 5

questions.question: What is the difference in environmental requirements for dispensing between aseptic products that cannot be sterile filtered (such as sterile powders or suspensions) and ingredients that will still be filtered or terminally sterilized later?

options.A: Both need only ISO 8/Grade C, differing only in records, sign-off and personnel training
options.B: The former must be ISO 5/Grade A, usually with separation technology; the latter at least ISO 8/Grade C
options.C: The former can be dispensed in ISO 8/Grade C, while the latter must be in ISO 5/Grade A with separation technology
options.D: Both must be in ISO 5/Grade A and always dispensed centrally

questions.explanation: Ingredients that will go through a later sterilization step (filtration or terminal sterilization) are usually dispensed in ISO 8/Grade C with local HEPA unidirectional airflow protection and aseptic technique; aseptic products that cannot be sterile filtered must be dispensed in ISO 5/Grade A, generally with separation technology isolating the operators.

questions.question: Which statement about the typical use of centralized and decentralized dispensing is correct?

options.A: Centralized is mostly for liquid raw materials; decentralized is mostly for dispensing solid and powder raw materials
options.B: Both are used only for solids, the difference being whether ERP is used to track raw materials
options.C: Decentralized needs no personnel training, so its mix-up risk is always lowest
options.D: Centralized is mostly for solids; decentralized is mostly for dispensing liquids in the compounding room

questions.explanation: Centralized dispensing is mostly limited to solid active ingredients and excipients; decentralized dispensing is mostly for liquids, dispensed within the production area (compounding room). For single-product compounding the latter also helps reduce mix-up and cross-contamination risk because only the designated materials are handled.

questions.question: When a cart from an automated autoclave or oven is removed from the chamber into an ISO 7/Grade B room, what protection does the guide require?

options.A: Push the cart directly into an unclassified corridor so items cool naturally before packaging
options.B: As long as the outer wrapping of the cart is intact, no additional airflow protection is needed
options.C: Provide local unidirectional ISO 5/Grade A airflow at the chamber exit so items stay protected until cooled
options.D: Move the cart to an ISO 8/Grade C room to cool, to reduce particle generation and save space

questions.explanation: Items removed from a sterilizer must maintain sterility continuity. If the cart is pulled into an ISO 7/Grade B room, local unidirectional ISO 5/Grade A airflow should be provided at the chamber exit so the items remain controlled while the load cools; the cart itself should also be qualified and periodically monitored.

questions.question: An aseptic product cannot be sterile filtered or otherwise sterilized after compounding. According to the guide, how should the addition of raw materials be controlled?

options.A: Add them in ISO 5/Grade A, preferably using RABS or a closed isolator
options.B: Add them openly in ISO 8/Grade C, controlling risk with SOPs and operator technique
options.C: Add them in ISO 7/Grade B, using higher airflow velocity to blow away dust
options.D: As long as single-use containers are used, there is no restriction on the addition environment

questions.explanation: If the product cannot be sterilized after compounding, the addition step is the last chance for exposure, so it must be in ISO 5/Grade A, preferably with RABS or a closed isolator. When handling fine powders, an airflow velocity below 0.45 m/s may help give better control.

questions.question: Which statement about sterile filtration is correct?

options.A: It effectively removes endotoxin, so upstream bioburden need not be controlled
options.B: It is suitable for all products and takes priority over terminal sterilization
options.C: It reduces endotoxin only to a limited extent, so the upstream solution must be kept at low bioburden
options.D: The final filter should be located as far as possible from the compounding or filling point, to reduce contamination and pressure drop risk

questions.explanation: Sterile filtration provides a defined reduction in microbial load but has limited effect on endotoxin, so low upstream bioburden must be ensured to limit endotoxin formation; the final filter should be as close as possible to the compounding or filling point, and is used only when terminal sterilization is not possible.

questions.question: When should the integrity of a sterilizing-grade filter membrane be confirmed with a validated method?

options.A: Only after use, with no need to test integrity again before use
options.B: Only once at the annual periodic revalidation, with the records kept properly
options.C: Only by the bubble point method, with all other validated methods rejected
options.D: Both before and after use, and methods such as bubble point may be used

questions.explanation: The guide requires membrane integrity to be confirmed with a validated method both before and after use, with methods including bubble point, diffusion/forward flow or water intrusion. EU Annex 1 recommends testing before sterilization so that a damaged cartridge is not missed, but this can affect downstream sterility, so a risk assessment is needed and redundant filters can reduce the risk.

questions.question: A depyrogenation tunnel needs the residence time of containers in the hot zone adjusted. According to the guide, which parameter most directly controls residence time?

options.A: Belt speed
options.B: The airflow pressure differential setting between the hot zone and the cooling zone
options.C: The water temperature, volume and flow rate used in the WFI washing stage
options.D: The replacement interval and frequency of the high-temperature UAF filters

questions.explanation: The tunnel has heating, dwell and cooling zones; the residence time in the dwell zone together with the set temperature (commonly 250 °C to 350 °C) achieves the required degree of depyrogenation, and residence time is usually controlled by belt speed. The cooling zone must cool down enough not to affect the product or deflect the exit UAF.

questions.question: Why are extra measures needed to protect sterility when capping is carried out outside the aseptic zone?

options.A: After capping the stopper no longer needs any integrity assessment
options.B: Until the aluminum cap is crimped the closure system is not yet complete, so LP/GAAS and stopper detection are needed
options.C: The capping area must be maintained at ISO 5/Grade A to avoid generating particles and microbial contamination
options.D: The aluminum cap itself is not sterile, so it must be applied in a Grade D area

questions.explanation: EU Annex 1 states that an aseptically filled vial is not fully integral until the aluminum cap is crimped onto the stoppered vial. If capping is done outside the aseptic zone, it must be protected by LP/GAAS, and laser or camera-based detection of raised or missing stoppers should reject nonconforming containers before capping.

questions.question: Comparing the Open Parison (shuttle) and Closed Parison (rotary/reciprocating) types of BFS, which statement is correct?

options.A: Closed Parison is the only type that can insert components, and it has the smallest footprint and the highest output
options.B: Open Parison has the highest output and greatly reduces plastic waste
options.C: Open Parison is more flexible for product changeover and suits small batches, and is the only type that can insert components
options.D: The two do not differ in batch size or flexibility, only in the mold material

questions.explanation: In Open Parison (shuttle) the molds move between the forming zone and the aseptic filling zone; it is more flexible for product changes, suits smaller batches, and is the only type that can insert components; Closed Parison has higher output, a larger footprint, and significantly reduces plastic waste.
questions.reference: ISPE Vol.3 §3.2.4 › Blow, Fill, and Seal

questions.question: Which statement about the F0 requirements of terminal sterilization processes is correct?

options.A: Full overkill is F0 >= 8; adjunct is F0 >= 15
options.B: Full overkill is F0 >= 15; adjunct is F0 >= 8
options.C: Both processes require only F0 >= 12, with no further distinction between overkill and adjunct
options.D: An adjunct process needs no F0 target, only continuous monitoring of chamber temperature

questions.explanation: The guide explains that terminal sterilization can be full overkill (F0 >= 15), or adjunct (F0 >= 8) for products that cannot withstand a full overkill; both have the same goal of meeting the requirement for the probability of a non-sterile unit (PNSU), so pre-sterilization bioburden must also be validated and routinely monitored.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using air over-pressure (air ballasting) when terminally sterilizing liquid-filled containers?

options.A: To speed up cooling and shorten the F0 accumulation time and cycle
options.B: To remove residual endotoxin contamination from the chamber and container surfaces
options.C: To make F0 identical at all locations, removing the need for temperature distribution testing
options.D: To reduce the pressure difference between the inside and outside of the containers and the chamber, protecting container integrity

questions.explanation: During sterilization the pressure difference between the container interior and the chamber can affect container integrity, and air over-pressure reduces this difference, especially for prefilled syringes and plastic containers. Container internal pressure changes with internal temperature, so the overpressure must be adjusted through the cycle accordingly.

questions.question: Comparing the two types of autoclave used for terminal sterilization, which statement is correct?

options.A: Air steam mix is mostly used for small volumes; the shower type is mostly used for large volumes and has faster heat-up and cool-down
options.B: Air steam mix is often used for large-volume items; the shower type is used only for small volumes and has slower heat-up and cool-down
options.C: Both use directly injected steam, differing only in the size of the autoclave
options.D: The shower type heats indirectly, so the quality of the heating water need not be considered

questions.explanation: Air steam mix injects clean steam together with sterile-filtered air and uses fans or nozzles to even out temperature, and is generally used for small volumes; the superheated water shower heats indirectly through an external heat exchanger and circulates a spray, is often used for large volumes, and has faster heat-up and cool-down and better temperature uniformity, but the heating water must still be of known quality (such as distilled or purified water).

questions.question: Why should inspection of containers for particulates, cosmetic defects and integrity be performed "after" terminal sterilization?

options.A: Because only after sterilization is there enough space to set up the inspection equipment and workstations
options.B: Because sterilization eliminates all defects, so inspection is only a formality
options.C: Because the sterilization process itself may affect these attributes, and the inspection must reflect the final state
options.D: Because regulations require that this kind of inspection be performed only by fully automated machines after sterilization

questions.explanation: The guide explains that inspection should be performed after terminal sterilization because the process can affect attributes such as particulates, appearance and container integrity. The expectation of USP <790> is that every finished unit is inspected to confirm freedom from particulates and from container or closure defects that could compromise sterility.
questions.reference: ISPE Vol.3 §3.2.7 (container inspection after terminal sterilization); §3.2.8

questions.question: In inspection validation using the Knapp method, what does "Reject Zone Efficiency (RZE)" measure?

options.A: The proportion of normal containers wrongly rejected, that is, the false reject rate
options.B: The degree of assurance that containers that "must be rejected" are actually rejected
options.C: The number of containers the machine can inspect per hour, that is, throughput
options.D: The results of inspectors' near-vision and color-vision tests, that is, a measure of eyesight

questions.explanation: The Knapp method classifies containers by Probability of Rejection; RZE describes the degree of assurance that "must-reject" containers are rejected. Both manual and automated inspection must be confirmed to reject nonconforming containers adequately (high RZE) while keeping the false reject rate acceptable.

questions.question: According to the guide, steam sterilization (autoclave or SIP) is usually validated as an overkill process. What are its minimum F0 and biological indicator requirements?

options.A: Minimum F0 of 15 minutes; Bacillus subtilis spores at 10^6 as the challenge organism, with no other biological indicators
options.B: Minimum F0 of 8 minutes; an overkill process need not use biological indicators
options.C: Minimum F0 of 12 minutes; endotoxin at 10^6 EU as the challenge
options.D: Minimum F0 of 12 minutes; it must be shown to inactivate Geobacillus stearothermophilus at 10^6

questions.explanation: Steam sterilization is usually confirmed as an overkill process, requiring a minimum F0 of 12 minutes and demonstrated inactivation of Geobacillus stearothermophilus (minimum population 1.0 x 10^6). Steam quality, venting, condensate removal and cycle design must also be confirmed.

questions.question: What is the guide's view on the control of endotoxin?

options.A: Filtration and moist heat sterilization have limited effect, so bioburden control, cleaning and depyrogenation must be combined
options.B: Moist heat sterilization effectively destroys endotoxin, needs no other steps, and suits all products
options.C: Sterilizing-grade filters retain most endotoxin, so filtration alone is enough
options.D: As long as filling is in ISO 5/Grade A, endotoxin need not be considered

questions.explanation: A note in the guide states that endotoxin is not significantly retained by most sterilizing-grade filters and is not significantly reduced by moist heat sterilization, so a combined approach is used: bioburden control, cleaning, dry heat depyrogenation and filtration.
questions.reference: ISPE Vol.3 §3.2.10 › Cleaning of Critical Parts (Note)

questions.question: Which of the following limitations of single-use systems does the guide explicitly mention?

options.A: They need no extractables/leachables assessment at all, because the materials are all medical grade
options.B: The film temperature limits may exclude processes that require heating, and the consumables make operating costs higher
options.C: Their implementation time is usually shorter than the facility concept design
options.D: They suit all product types, so no risk assessment is needed

questions.explanation: Single-use can remove cleaning validation and reduce operator exposure to highly active substances, but film temperature limits may rule out products that need heating, consumables raise operating costs, and introduction requires cross-functional work on suppliers, design, extractables/leachables and integrity testing, usually taking much longer than the facility design phase.

questions.question: Which statement about the unloading location of sterilized items is consistent with the guide?

options.A: Isolator-based facilities can unload to Grade C; RABS-based facilities usually unload to Grade A
options.B: Both types of facility must unload items into an unclassified area before disinfection
options.C: Isolator-based facilities must unload to Grade A; RABS-based facilities can unload to Grade C
options.D: The unloading location is unrelated to the barrier technology used in the facility and is decided by the equipment vendor

questions.explanation: The guide explains that in isolator-based facilities items can enter the isolator through an RTP or an automated VHP airlock, so the autoclave can unload to ISO 8/Grade C; in RABS-based facilities the autoclave usually unloads into an ISO 5/Grade A area to maintain sterility continuity.

questions.question: Which of the following pairings of a sterilization or decontamination method with its typical use is correct?

options.A: VHP for depyrogenating glass containers; gamma for sterilizing SIP piping
options.B: EtO for decontaminating the inside of isolators; VHP for sterilizing prefilled syringes
options.C: Gamma for routine cleaning of lyophilizers; EtO for sterilizing WFI systems and disinfecting piping
options.D: VHP for isolator decontamination; gamma for single-use and RTU components

questions.explanation: VHP is typically used to decontaminate the inside of barrier isolators; gamma irradiation is typically used for single-use technology and some RTU elastomeric components (such as syringe plungers), with cycles validated and routine dose audits; EtO is typically used for pre-nested ready-to-fill syringes, vials and cartridges.

questions.question: What three approaches to product protection in facility design does the guide list, and which does it recommend as preferred?

options.A: Separation by space, procedure and cost; separation by procedure is recommended as preferred
options.B: Separation by space, time and personnel; separation by time is recommended as preferred
options.C: Separation by space, procedure and time; separation by space is preferred where feasible
options.D: Separation by procedure, equipment and time; the three need not be ranked, and each site chooses

questions.explanation: The guide explains that product protection has traditionally relied on separation by procedure, space or time (campaign), or a combination, and recommends using spatial separation, such as isolators and RABS, to maintain the ISO 5/Grade A environment where practical, because this is more robust than relying on procedures.

questions.question: How do the requirements for the rooms surrounding a RABS and an isolator differ?

options.A: A RABS is surrounded by ISO 7/Grade B, with LP/GAAS at the door side; the isolator room can be lowered to ISO 8/Grade C
options.B: A RABS can be surrounded by ISO 8/Grade C; an isolator must be surrounded by ISO 7/Grade B with a double airlock
options.C: Both must be surrounded by ISO 5/Grade A to maintain sterility
options.D: Neither a RABS nor an isolator has any classification requirement for the surrounding room

questions.explanation: Most RABS interventions are through glove ports, but doors are occasionally opened, so the surroundings must be ISO 7/Grade B, with the space where doors open meeting LP/GAAS; the inside of an isolator is a fully closed, isolated environment, which allows lower room classification, gowning requirements, number of airlocks and cleaning scope, but it is still at least ISO 8/Grade C.

questions.question: What is the main role of the zoning and transition diagram in the layout programming process?

options.A: To list the area and budget of every room as a purchasing list for equipment
options.B: To select equipment vendors and machine models, and complete equipment acceptance
options.C: To replace the block flow diagram, so that the latter no longer needs to be produced and updated during design
options.D: To define the transition requirements and airflow directions between different classified areas, serving as the "rules" the layout must follow

questions.explanation: The programming steps in the guide are objectives, block flow diagram and facility program, zoning and transition diagram, and then the concept layout. The zoning and transition diagram identifies all the areas that affect the space and their relationships, and defines classification transitions and directional airflow, which become the basis for the layout.

questions.question: A facility can provide only one shared gowning room for personnel both entering and leaving the aseptic area. Which practice is acceptable according to the guide?

options.A: Allow entering and leaving personnel to use it at the same time, to shorten the waiting queue
options.B: Gowning and degowning are not done at the same time, with time allowed for air purging
options.C: Provide airflow only for degowning, and turn it off for gowning to save energy
options.D: Put up a sign at the door, with no procedural restrictions on use

questions.explanation: The guide recommends separate entry and exit routes for ISO 7/Grade B and higher aseptic areas; if a shared gowning room is used for two-way traffic, gowning and degowning must not be done at the same time, and there must be adequate air purge time. Simultaneous use would let contaminated discarded garments affect the clean garments of people who are about to gown.

questions.question: Which statement about drains and sinks is consistent with the guide?

options.A: As long as an air break is provided, an open sink can be installed in a Grade B area, but floor drains are still not allowed
options.B: Rooms of ISO 8/Grade C or higher should adjoin an exterior wall, for natural light, ventilation and drainage
options.C: Open sinks and floor drains must not be installed in Grade A/B areas
options.D: A central vacuum system needs no backflow preventer, to avoid adding pressure loss

questions.explanation: The guide states explicitly that open sinks and floor drains are not allowed in ISO 7/Grade B and ISO 5/Grade A areas; portable vacuum cleaners with HEPA filters can be used, and a central vacuum system must have a backflow preventer. Rooms of ISO 8/Grade C or cleaner also should not adjoin an exterior wall (because of moisture, pests and the effect of wind on room pressure).

questions.question: Which statement about the "improvement step" and the transition line when materials move from a lower classified area to a higher one is correct?

options.A: An improvement step can be removal of outer packaging, wiping or fumigation; a transition line is recommended in airlocks
options.B: An improvement step applies only to personnel gowning, and materials need no treatment
options.C: A transition line is used only in Grade D and lower airlocks, and is never provided in Grade C and higher airlocks
options.D: Materials need no cleaning before crossing a transition line, and pass once the quantity is recorded

questions.explanation: The guide expects an "improvement step" when personnel and materials move from a lower to a higher classification: for materials it can be cleaning or disinfection, removal of outer packaging, hand wiping or fumigation decontamination; for personnel it can be an additional layer of protective garments. A transition line is recommended in airlocks entering ISO 8/Grade C and higher.

questions.topic: Access to Grade A and B
questions.question: Which statement about entry to areas of different grades is consistent with the guide?

options.A: Grade A can be entered directly from Grade C without passing through a Grade B area, to shorten the route
options.B: A double-door interlocked airlock must be provided between Grade A and Grade B as a separation
options.C: Personnel and materials entering Grade B can share the same entry airlock
options.D: Grade A can be entered only from Grade B; Grade B is entered from Grade C through an airlock

questions.explanation: The guide requires step-by-step transitions: ISO 5/Grade A is entered only from ISO 7/Grade B, usually without an airlock between them but with clear visual indication and a physical barrier; entry to ISO 7/Grade B is from ISO 8/Grade C through an airlock, and personnel and materials should have their own entry airlocks.

questions.question: According to the guide, how should the direction of door opening generally be considered?

options.A: Doors should open toward the lower-pressure room, to reduce the air conditioning energy load and supply air volume
options.B: Door swing does not affect pressure differentials, and can be decided entirely on appearance, traffic flow and ease of construction
options.C: Doors usually open toward the high-pressure side, but egress regulations take priority, and Grade B and above need a risk assessment
options.D: All doors should have manual handles, so cleaning staff actually touch and disinfect them

questions.explanation: The guide states that doors should usually open toward the higher-pressure side to help maintain the pressure differential, but egress regulations often take priority; if a door opens toward an ISO 7/Grade B or higher area, a risk assessment is needed because the door has been exposed to a lower classified area. Hardware should also be easy to clean, and touch-free door openers are recommended.

questions.question: What does the guide require for cleanroom surface materials and floor drains?

options.A: Materials that are porous and absorbent are preferred, so particles do not become airborne
options.B: Non-shedding, non-porous and resistant to microorganisms; coved corners; no floor drains in aseptic process areas
options.C: Corners should be square for precise construction; floor drains may also be installed in Grade B areas to aid drainage
options.D: Visual appearance is enough, and resistance to cleaning agents need not be considered

questions.explanation: The guide requires finishes that are non-shedding, non-porous and resistant to microbial growth, with smooth, easy-to-clean surfaces; corners between wall, ceiling and floor need an adequate radius, and the finishes must withstand repeated cleaning and disinfection. Floor drains are not allowed in aseptic process areas, and elsewhere should be minimized and use a recessed air break of at least 2 inches.

questions.question: A batch of materials must be decontaminated with a chemical disinfectant with a specified dwell time. According to the guide, how should the airlock design handle this?

options.A: Materials and personnel share one airlock, and processing is completed after shortening the dwell time
options.B: No airlock is provided, and the materials are left in the corridor to be disinfected
options.C: A separate airlock must be provided, large enough to hold the materials during the disinfection dwell time
options.D: The personnel gowning room replaces the material airlock, handling personnel and materials together

questions.explanation: When material decontamination involves a chemical disinfectant dwell time, the guide explicitly requires a separate airlock to be provided; the airlock must also be large enough to hold the materials during the dwell without interfering with personnel movement or airflow. Smaller items can use a pass box instead of a material airlock.

questions.question: An autoclave, tunnel or washer has openings on two sides, and its mechanical support space can be entered from a cleanroom. According to the guide, how should the service access and pressure be arranged?

options.A: Enter from the less clean side, seal the critical side, and keep the service space at negative pressure
options.B: Enter from the cleaner side, and keep the service space at relative positive pressure to prevent backflow
options.C: Entering from either side is acceptable, and the service space pressure needs no special specification
options.D: Enter directly from the aseptic area for convenient loading and unloading, and keep it at positive pressure

questions.explanation: The guide explains that the mechanical service space of such equipment should be entered from the less clean side, with a tight seal on the critical side, and these service spaces should be kept at negative pressure relative to the areas they connect to, so that maintenance activity does not contaminate the clean areas.

questions.question: Which statement about walkable ceilings is correct?

options.A: They must be used frequently during production, so HEPA filters can be replaced promptly
options.B: They may be installed only directly above Grade A areas, and are prohibited above any other class
options.C: They require maintenance staff to enter the cleanroom to carry out overhead repairs
options.D: They are an ideal solution for overhead maintenance, but entry may be prohibited during production because walking can shed particles

questions.explanation: A walkable ceiling lets people carry out overhead maintenance without entering the cleanroom, but walking can cause particles to fall, so regulated companies may prohibit access above the processing area during production.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Process Corridor in the concept diagram?

options.A: A one-way passage dedicated to the transport of exposed product, where no personnel may pass
options.B: A parallel passage shared by non-product-exposed items and personnel, avoiding airlocks in series
options.C: An unclassified external corridor with no direct connection to the production traffic flow
options.D: A central passage where all waste and finished product share the same route

questions.explanation: The text explains that the Process Corridor is a shared parallel path for all non-product-exposed items and personnel, mainly connecting the gowning rooms and the ISO 8/Grade C production suites, and is also used for material entry; it avoids cumbersome airlocks in series while maintaining step-by-step transitions.

questions.question: In the concept diagrams, which statement about the capping location and whether aluminum caps need to be sterilized is correct?

options.A: Wherever capping is done, the aluminum caps need no prior sterilization
options.B: Wherever capping is done, the aluminum caps must be sterilized before use
options.C: Capping inside an isolator requires sterilized aluminum caps; capping in a Grade C RABS with LP/GAAS does not
options.D: Capping inside an isolator needs no sterilization; capping inside a RABS always requires sterilized aluminum caps

questions.explanation: The figure shows capping carried out inside the isolator, so the aluminum caps should be sterilized; another configuration has the product leave the ISO 5/Grade A isolator and be capped under LP/GAAS in a RABS in ISO 8/Grade C, where the caps need not be sterilized, and particles from capping are blocked by the positive pressure of the isolator and the outflow air at the mousehole.
questions.reference: ISPE Vol.3 §4.8, Figure 4.5 and Figure 4.7 notes

questions.question: If waste cannot be treated as a closed system, how do the concept diagrams recommend achieving separation?

options.A: Transport it at the same time and by the same route as finished product, to save labor and time
options.B: By procedural means, or by removal through the Process Corridor outside production hours (time separation)
options.C: Place it directly in a bin inside the Grade A area for temporary storage, to be cleared together after the whole batch ends
options.D: Never remove it until the end of the whole product lifecycle, and dispose of it all at once

questions.explanation: The figure note states that waste that cannot be treated as closed is an open system, and can be separated by procedural means or by transport through the Process Corridor outside production hours; this is time separation.

questions.question: Which statement about the factors affecting HVAC cost in a sterile facility is consistent with the guide?

options.A: Isolators can lower room classification and so reduce HVAC size; redundancy is decided by failure mode risk analysis
options.B: Using isolators actually increases room classification needs, making HVAC larger and costlier
options.C: All HVAC equipment must have 100% redundancy, with no risk analysis needed
options.D: The more complex the design, the more it reduces failure risk and lowers total cost

questions.explanation: The guide points out that isolators and other microenvironments (RABS, LP/GAAS) can reduce classification needs and particle challenge, making the HVAC smaller and cheaper; redundancy should be decided by failure mode risk analysis and usually does not require duplicating all equipment; an overly complex scheme costs more and also carries a higher risk of failure.

questions.question: Which statement about the in operation and at rest conditions is correct?

options.A: In operation is with no personnel and equipment shut down; at rest is normal production operation
options.B: Both require personnel to be present, differing only in whether product is present
options.C: At rest requires equipment to be running, but does not require the HVAC to be running
options.D: In operation has product, equipment and personnel; at rest has no product and no personnel

questions.explanation: The guide recommends that in operation (dynamic) be consistent with the ISO definition: HVAC and local protection devices running, product or simulated product present, equipment operating and the specified personnel present. At rest (static) is HVAC running, no product or personnel, and equipment not operating; EU Annex 1 sets particle limits for both states.

questions.question: Which statement about recovery testing is correct?

options.A: It applies to all classifications, including UAF areas of ISO 5/Grade A
options.B: It measures only the performance of the HVAC itself, and is not affected by room activity and personnel
options.C: It measures the time to fall from in operation back to the at rest limit; it does not apply to UAF spaces
options.D: It measures the time to rise from at rest to the in operation limit, and applies to all classifications

questions.explanation: Recovery time records the time for the particle concentration to fall from in operation to the corresponding at rest limit; a challenge agent can also be used to raise the concentration to or above the in operation limit, giving more data. A UAF space has a very high air change rate and clears particles extremely quickly, so recovery and air change do not apply.

questions.question: Which description of LP/GAAS is consistent with the guide?

options.A: LP and GAAS are synonymous, and ISO 5 should be achieved 100-150 mm below the filter face
options.B: LP and GAAS are different classes, and may be used only at Grade A or above
options.C: It can be used only with a Grade B background, and not in Grade D background areas
options.D: The at rest and in operation limits are already uniformly specified by ISO 14644

questions.explanation: The guide treats Local Protection and Grade A Air Supply as equivalent, usually with terminal HEPA filters near the work area; the supply air should achieve ISO 5 (0.5 and 5.0 um) at 100-150 mm below the filter face. It can be used with any background classification (including Grade D); its at rest and in operation limits are often overlooked, and must be set at design time, otherwise the qualification phase is easily delayed.

questions.topic: Air change rate as planning tool
questions.question: FDA guidance states that 20 ACH is generally acceptable for ISO 8 (0.5 um, in operation). How does the guide recommend using ACH?

options.A: Treat 20 ACH as the legal minimum air change value applicable to all classifications
options.B: Use ACH as a planning tool, with measured particle and viable counts as the acceptance criteria
options.C: Completely prohibit using ACH as any kind of reference in the design phase
options.D: Use ACH to replace all the measurement work of environmental monitoring and qualification

questions.explanation: ACH has traditionally been used to specify dilution airflow and was matched to cleanliness, but ISO 14644-4 and IEST-RP-CC012 no longer correlate them this way. The guide recommends using ACH as a planning tool and using measured room particle counts, viable counts or other measured indicators as the acceptance criteria.

questions.question: Unless the product has other requirements, what comfortable relative humidity (RH) range does ISPE Vol. 3 recommend for aseptic manufacturing areas?

options.A: 20-25% RH, because low humidity reduces microbial growth and human shedding, applicable to all aseptic areas
options.B: 30-60% RH; the lower limit may be relaxed in dry, cold climates, but below 25% is not recommended
options.C: 40-70% RH, because below 70% there is no risk of mold growth, and static is suppressed
options.D: 60-80% RH, because higher humidity reduces static and particle adhesion without promoting mold

questions.explanation: The document recommends a comfortable humidity of 30-60% RH; below 25% is not recommended because static causes particles to cling to non-conductive surfaces and be shed in large numbers when disturbed. RH above 70% may over time grow mold, and good practice is to stay below 60%, so high humidity is not a good choice.

questions.question: Which statement about the minimum recommended values for the pressure cascade is correct?

options.A: Minimum 5 Pa between rooms of different grades; at least 10-15 Pa between rooms of the same grade
options.B: About 25 Pa between rooms of different grades; about 12.5 Pa between rooms of the same grade, measured with the doors open
options.C: Regardless of grade, all adjacent rooms must reach 45 Pa or more, whether or not the doors are closed
options.D: 10-15 Pa between rooms of different grades (doors closed); minimum 5 Pa between rooms of the same grade

questions.explanation: The guidance recommends a minimum of 10-15 Pa between different grades (doors closed), with a typical design value of 12.5 +/- 2.5 Pa per step; between rooms of the same grade a minimum of 5 Pa is enough. The statement "Minimum 5 Pa between rooms of different grades; at least 10-15 Pa between rooms of the same grade" reverses the two values; and the maximum room pressure in a simple facility is usually also below 45 Pa (relative to the building), which is not a requirement for each step.

questions.question: The air inlet of an active RABS is located high on the side of the machine, and an on-site smoke test finds poor airflow patterns around it. According to ISPE Vol. 3, what is the better approach?

options.A: Remove the RABS air through a low-level return in the room, and confirm with CFD simulation
options.B: Move the inlet to a higher position, so air flushes the whole room from top to bottom
options.C: Add movable baffles so the high-level inlet opens only during personnel interventions
options.D: Raise the room air change rate until particle counts are below the ISO 5/Grade A limit, and keep the inlet position unchanged

questions.explanation: For either a passive or an active RABS, the best practice is for the RABS air to leave the room through a low-level return rather than being drawn in through a high side inlet; a high-level inlet seriously disturbs the airflow pattern around the RABS. The document also recommends confirming airflow by CFD simulation. Increasing air changes alone does not fix a poor airflow pattern.

questions.question: From an HVAC viewpoint, one of the biggest differences between an isolator and a RABS is that an isolator has multiple operating modes. What are the four main HVAC operating modes of an isolator?

options.A: Outflow, Decontamination, Aeration, Standby
options.B: Inflow, Decontamination, Recirculation, Operation
options.C: Outflow, Decontamination, Aeration, Operation
options.D: Setup, Decontamination, Aeration, Idle

questions.explanation: The document lists four modes: Outflow (HEPA air flushes the critical zone and flows out through open doors, used for cleaning and setup), Decontamination (the room is sealed and gaseous decontaminant circulated), Aeration (HEPA air is exhausted through the exhaust), and Operation (HEPA air flows into the surrounding room through the mousehole). By contrast, a RABS has only one operating mode from an HVAC viewpoint.

questions.question: What range of cleanroom "recovery time" (from in use back to at rest) does EU GMP suggest as acceptable, and when does timing start?

options.A: 5 to 10 minutes, timed from the last acceptable particle count
options.B: 15 to 20 minutes, timed from when room activity stops
options.C: 30 to 45 minutes, timed from the completion of cleaning and disinfection
options.D: 60 minutes or more, timed from the restart of the HVAC

questions.explanation: The document explains that recovery time is the time for a room to return from in use particle levels to at rest levels, counted from when room activity stops; EU GMP suggests 15 to 20 minutes as acceptable. It is a good indicator of the overall robustness of the air conditioning system.

questions.question: According to ISPE Vol. 3, what is the typical frequency of integrity testing for terminal HEPA filters?

options.A: Twice a year for aseptic filling environments; once every one to two years for less critical areas, with the frequency supported by data
options.B: Once a month for aseptic filling environments; once a year for less critical areas, with no additional justification or data needed
options.C: Once every five years in all areas, in step with airflow pattern testing and decided by the supplier
options.D: Only after an HVAC failure or filter replacement, with no periodic testing or data support needed

questions.explanation: The document suggests that integrity testing of terminal HEPA filters is typically twice a year for aseptic filling environments and once every one to two years for less critical areas, and that the rationale for the frequency should be supported by ongoing data. When testing HEPA filters, the velocity and uniformity at the face of ISO 5/Grade A and LP/GAAS filters should also be confirmed.

questions.question: A room's differential pressure must be controlled to +/- 2.5 Pa. According to the principle in the document, what accuracy should the pressure differential instrument ideally have?

options.A: +/- 2.5 Pa, the same as the control range
options.B: +/- 1.0 Pa, about 40% of the control range
options.C: +/- 0.25 Pa, about 10% of the control range
options.D: +/- 0.025 Pa, about 1% of the control range

questions.explanation: The document states that the instrument should use the smallest applicable range, and its error should be only a small fraction (generally 10%) of the resolution required; for example, when controlling to +/- 2.5 Pa, an accuracy of 0.25 Pa is ideal. Drift must also be considered, and the calibration frequency must be enough to control it.

questions.question: To choose a central reference point for pressure differential measurement in an aseptic area, which location is most suitable?

options.A: An outdoor area outside the building, because it is completely unaffected by indoor airflow and door opening
options.B: The mechanical room, because it is close to the air conditioning equipment and wiring is convenient
options.C: A corridor next to a supply air outlet, because pressure is stable and airflow data are easy to obtain
options.D: A large, stable space with few doors and constant ventilation, such as an interstitial area

questions.explanation: The reference point should be in a large, stable space with few doors, and an interstitial area is often a good choice. The outdoors is poor because it is affected by wind velocity pressure, and a mechanical room is often poor because of its constant-temperature ventilation; sensors should also be kept away from doors and supply and return openings.

questions.question: A plant wants to reduce airflow when rooms are not in use to save energy (idle airflow setback). According to the document, which practice is correct?

options.A: Reduce airflow as soon as room activity stops, and also turn off pressure and humidity control to save more energy, restarting on recovery
options.B: Reduce airflow only 15-20 minutes after activity stops, keep pressure and temperature/humidity control, and validate setback performance and recovery time
options.C: Manually record the pressure once per shift during setback, with no need to validate the time to recover service or maintain temperature and humidity control
options.D: Reducing the room airflow to zero in setback is safest, because no personnel and equipment generate particles then, and no pressure control need be maintained

questions.explanation: Setback reduces airflow for rooms that are not in use (no personnel, no production, setup or cleaning), usually starting 15-20 minutes after use stops to let the room recover first, and keeps pressure and temperature/humidity control to preserve aseptic conditions. Both the performance in the setback state and the time to return to service should be validated, and measuring room airflow is also recommended when variable airflow is used.

questions.question: Which statement about the qualification scope of the HVAC automatic control system (BAS/BMS) and the environmental monitoring system (EMS) in ISPE Vol. 3 is correct?

options.A: HVAC controls themselves need not be qualified, and their performance is monitored by a qualified EMS; only shared field devices need qualification
options.B: All HVAC controllers and field devices must be fully qualified, otherwise they may not be used in any aseptic or support area, and must be fully revalidated every year
options.C: Only temperature and humidity control need qualification, while pressure control, alarms and data recording functions do not, with no checks needed
options.D: The EMS needs to be qualified only once at initial installation, and afterwards is not subject to 21 CFR Part 11 or change control

questions.explanation: The document explains that automatic controllers may indirectly affect patient safety and product quality, but their performance can be monitored by a qualified EMS, so HVAC controls need not be qualified; only when control and environmental monitoring are shared do the field devices need qualification. The EMS should comply with 21 CFR Part 11 and be validated to ensure the accuracy of readings and records.

questions.topic: Process vs Process Support compressed air
questions.question: In the utility classification of ISPE Vol. 3, which of the following is usually classified as a Process System (rather than a Process Support System)?

options.A: Instrument air used for pneumatic valves (no product contact)
options.B: Clearly labeled breathing air for operators
options.C: Chilled water supplied to HVAC and cooling coils
options.D: Filtered sterile compressed air used for the sterilization step after SIP or to push product to the filling machine

questions.explanation: Compressed air may be Process or Process Support depending on its use: filtered sterile compressed air used for sterilization after SIP or to push product to filling is usually classified as a Process System; instrument air, breathing air and chilled water have no product contact, are Process Support, and are designed per GEP.

questions.question: What does ISPE Vol. 3 recommend for the filtration of process gases (such as nitrogen and compressed air) used in aseptic processes?

options.A: Pre-filtration at 0.2 um or better; 5 um filtration at the point of use is enough
options.B: Pre-filtration at 5 um or better; a 0.2 um filter at the point of use for aseptic applications
options.C: Only one 0.45 um filter at the plant room outlet for the whole system, with no filtration at the point of use
options.D: Pre-filtration at 10 um; a 0.22 um filter added only at points of use where sampling is needed

questions.explanation: The document recommends a pre-filter pore size of 5 um or better; for sterile or aseptic applications, a 0.2 um filter is required at the point of use, and the filter and its downstream components must be sterilized or sanitized, with periodic in situ or off-line integrity testing. The statement "Pre-filtration at 0.2 um or better; 5 um filtration at the point of use is enough" reverses the roles of the two pore sizes.

questions.question: When pure steam (clean steam) is used directly to sterilize product-contact equipment and parts, which parameters does the document require to be tested periodically and controlled within specified ranges?

options.A: pH, conductivity and total organic carbon (TOC), tested batch by batch to the pharmacopeial specification for water for injection
options.B: Boiler additive concentration, water hardness and chloride content, spot-tested once per quarter
options.C: Non-condensable gases (NCG), dryness and superheat
options.D: Steam velocity, pipe diameter, number of steam traps and the design margin of steam pressure

questions.explanation: Pure steam should contain no boiler additives, and the condensate must meet the WFI specification; when used for direct sterilization, NCG, dryness and superheat must be tested periodically and controlled, with superheat minimized on entering the autoclave. The design should also slope the piping and reduce steam traps to avoid microbial growth in condensate.

questions.question: When nitrogen or instrument air used for pneumatic parts on a filling line is vented during aseptic processing, what does the document recommend?

options.A: Vent it to a non-critical area outside the equipment, with the venting location decided by a risk assessment
options.B: Vent it into the ISO 5/Grade A area, because airflow there is cleanest and dilutes it immediately
options.C: Vent it above the ISO 7/Grade B sterile corridor, so the return air carries it away
options.D: No special handling is needed, as long as the instrument air has been filtered at 0.2 um

questions.explanation: The document states that gases are vented at many points during operation, and if vented during aseptic processing they should go to a non-critical area outside the equipment, with the location decided by a risk assessment; instrument air should also be vented away from ISO 5/Grade A to maintain low particle and microbial levels.

questions.question: Heating and cooling systems are usually Process Support, but what point does the document still remind designers to watch?

options.A: As long as a food-grade heat transfer medium is used, leakage into the product does not affect quality, so the jacket need not be checked
options.B: Heat transfer medium piping should be placed above the aseptic area where possible, to shorten the distance to process equipment and reduce pipe length
options.C: Heating and cooling systems must have no monitoring, to avoid the sensors themselves causing leaks and contamination
options.D: If heat transfer fluid leaks from a jacket into a compounded batch, it contaminates the batch regardless of its nature

questions.explanation: The document stresses that indirect heat transfer equipment should not leak to the environment or product, that medium selection should consider the leak risk, and that pressure testing and level monitoring should be used to detect leaks; piping location also should not interfere with the aseptic area if a leak occurs. A jacket leak contaminates the batch regardless of the fluid's nature.

questions.question: What minimum illuminance does ISPE Vol. 3 recommend for the lighting of personnel work areas in manufacturing areas?

options.A: 100 lux, at 1 meter above the floor
options.B: 300 lux, at 1 meter above the floor
options.C: 500 lux, at 1 meter above the floor
options.D: 1000 lux, at 1 meter above the floor

questions.explanation: The document recommends that lighting in manufacturing areas be uniform, and that personnel work areas not be below 500 lux at one meter above the floor. Luminaires should also be cleanable, non-shedding, free of crevices or sealed, and should be kept from being placed directly above open processes.

questions.question: The document uses the word "sealed" in its GMP requirements for electrical equipment. How does its meaning differ between cleanliness classes?

options.A: In ISO 5/Grade A it means hermetically sealed; in ISO 8/Grade C it means a high degree of water and dust protection
options.B: In ISO 5/Grade A it means a high degree of water and dust protection; in ISO 8/Grade C it means hermetically sealed
options.C: In both classes it only needs to keep dust out, with no difference in degree, and only the IP rating needs to be marked
options.D: Only ISO 8/Grade C needs sealing, while ISO 5/Grade A should use no electrical equipment at all

questions.explanation: Although the criterion looks the same from ISO 5/Grade A to ISO 8/Grade C, the degree differs: in Grade A, sealed means hermetically sealed, while in Grade C it means a high level of water and dust protection. The document also recommends that electrical equipment in Grade A be reduced to an absolute minimum, for example by placing light switches outside the door in the corridor.

questions.question: If the doors of an airlock or gowning room are fitted with an electrical interlock, what does the document recommend?

options.A: The interlock must have no bypass function, so that personnel cannot break the pressure differential in an emergency; training should replace an override design, and a supervisor must approve each use
options.B: It should include an override function usable in an emergency, and this should be verified at commissioning/qualification
options.C: The interlock need be checked only once at annual validation, with no alarm in normal times and no verification at commissioning
options.D: The interlock can replace all pressure differential monitoring, so the facility need not provide pressure differential sensors nor verify them at validation

questions.explanation: Electrical interlocks help maintain pressure differentials and good GMP practice; the alternative is a local alarm when several doors are open at the same time. If an interlock is provided, it must have an override for emergencies, and verification at commissioning/qualification is recommended. An interlock cannot replace pressure differential monitoring.

questions.question: In the monitoring system for a CPP, what is the difference between an Alert Alarm and an Action Alarm?

options.A: Alert means Process Limits have been exceeded; Action means a deviation from Normal Operating Conditions
options.B: They mean the same thing, differing only in alarm sound volume and display color
options.C: Alert always requires an immediate shutdown; Action need only be noted in the batch record
options.D: Alert: deviation from Normal Operating Conditions; Action: deviation from Process Limits

questions.explanation: An Alert is an early warning, meaning the parameter has deviated from the normal operating range; an Action means Process Limits have been exceeded, which may cause a product quality problem. The document also requires that alarms be latched and not clear themselves until acknowledged by the operator, and that all alarm conditions be recorded with corrective action.

questions.question: In Vol. 3's description of instrument accuracy, what determines the "minimum accuracy requirement" of an instrument (the Instrument Permitted Limit), so that the true value still lies within the Process Limits when the reading is at the edge of the Alert Limits?

options.A: It is determined by the full width of the Process Limits, and the instrument uncertainty must not exceed that full width
options.B: It is determined by the full width of the Alert Limits, and the instrument uncertainty must not exceed that full width
options.C: It is determined by the difference between the Process Limits and the Alert Limits, and the uncertainty must not exceed that difference
options.D: It is fixed at 10% of the desired resolution, independent of the Process or Alert Limits

questions.explanation: The document states that the measurement uncertainty should not be greater than the difference between the Process Limits and the Alert Limits; this difference is the minimum accuracy requirement of the instrument (the Instrument Permitted Limit), and choosing a more accurate instrument allows for drift. The "10% of resolution" is the document's recommendation for differential pressure instruments, not this definition.

questions.question: According to the introduction in ISPE Vol. 3, what are the typical situations in which isolators and RABS are used in facility design?

options.A: RABS is usually used in new plant design and offers a higher safety level; the isolator is usually used in upgrades of existing facilities
options.B: The isolator is mostly used in new plant design and offers a higher safety level; RABS is often used in upgrades of existing facilities
options.C: Both apply only to large high-speed filling lines, and not to small clinical trial batches or multi-product facilities
options.D: Both apply only to non-hazardous products, and hazardous products may never use them

questions.explanation: The document explains that an isolator can provide a higher safety level and is usually used in new plants; RABS is often used in upgrades where the protection of existing equipment needs strengthening. Both technologies can be used from small clinical trial batches to large high-speed lines, and also for QC sterility testing and formulation compounding; for hazardous products, both help protect the operators because less air spills out.

questions.question: What are the main difference and typical use of a closed isolator versus an open isolator?

options.A: Closed exchanges air with the environment only through a microbial retentive filter and suits batch processes with few components; open is used for continuous processes, with mouseholes and a pressure differential maintaining outward airflow
options.B: Closed suits continuous processes and moves materials through mouseholes, maintaining outward airflow by pressure differential; open exchanges air only through a microbial retentive filter and suits batch processes with few components
options.C: Closed is always at negative pressure and open always at positive pressure, regardless of process type and filter grade
options.D: Closed can be placed only in an ISO 5/Grade A background and open must be in an ISO 8/Grade C background, regardless of process type

questions.explanation: By the definitions of PDA TR34, a closed isolator exchanges air with the environment only through a microbial retentive filter, with materials loaded before decontamination or transferred in through a decontamination airlock, and suits batch processes with few components; an open isolator can pass air directly to the environment through openings (such as mouseholes), is used for continuous processes, and uses pressure differentials between zones to ensure outward airflow.

questions.question: A site wants to handle a hazardous product in a RABS. Which type of RABS might be suitable, supported by a risk assessment?

options.A: A passive RABS, with air spilling into the room and returned through an ordinary HEPA filter
options.B: An active RABS with air spilling into the room (air overspill) and no separate return filter
options.C: An open RABS, with doors opened manually several times per shift for interventions and ordinary masks for protection, with no additional disinfection at interventions
options.D: An active RABS with air returned through HEPA and a safe change filter

questions.explanation: A RABS that spills air to the surroundings is not suitable for products requiring containment of hazardous substances. Only an active RABS with air returned through HEPA filters (using safe change filters at the return to protect operating and maintenance staff) may, based on a risk assessment, be suitable for hazardous products.

questions.question: To prevent contamination from entering through openings such as mouseholes, in what range is the isolator pressure differential relative to the surrounding environment usually maintained?
questions.explanation: The document states that an isolator should be maintained at positive pressure relative to its surroundings, typically 15-50 Pa, and the higher the pressure differential, the better the separation (ISO 14644-4 suggests an air velocity >= 0.2 m/s). But too high a differential creates strong airflow, which may disturb the UAF inside the enclosure or the process (such as powder filling or vials falling), and mouseholes may also see backflow at high velocity.

questions.question: A site wants to compare the labor and gowning costs of an isolator and a RABS. According to the document, which description is correct?

options.A: An isolator needs gowning only to suit a lower classified background, and one person can serve multiple functions; RABS operators still need full sterile gowning and are mostly limited to a single position
options.B: Operators of both isolators and RABS must wear full sterile gowns, with the same gowning cost, and one person cannot do multiple tasks
options.C: RABS operators can gown less and one person can serve multiple functions; an isolator instead needs more gowning and more labor, and the gowning grade can be lowered
options.D: Because an isolator is closed, operator entry needs more sterilization and degowning procedures, which reduces labor flexibility, and sterile gowning must be worn throughout

questions.explanation: An isolator removes the need for enclosed sterile gowns, hoods and masks, with gowning determined by the lower-grade background room, so one person can serve multiple functions and entry is not limited by sterile gowning, saving laundry and sterilization costs (4-5 sets of garments per person per day can be used). A RABS lacks these advantages, because operators need full sterile gowning and are mostly limited to a single position.

questions.question: When choosing the method of transferring materials into an isolator or RABS, what does the document typically require for bioburden reduction (log reduction)?

options.A: Both isolators and RABS usually require 6-log, regardless of surface bioburden
options.B: Isolator usually 3-log; RABS usually 6-log with liquid decontamination required, and both must be validated batch by batch
options.C: Isolator usually 2-log; RABS needs no log reduction, only visual cleanliness
options.D: Isolator usually 6-log (as low as 4-log for surfaces with very low bioburden); RABS usually 3-log

questions.explanation: The document says an isolator application usually requires a 6-log reduction (at least 4-log is acceptable for surfaces with very low bioburden), while RABS is usually fine with 3-log. The log reductions in the table are for reference only and must still be demonstrated in validation; if the transfer involves toxic compounds, a full risk assessment is needed.

questions.topic: Background environment for isolator vs RABS
questions.question: To comply with global regulations, what backgrounds are recommended for an isolator and for a RABS respectively?

options.A: Isolator in ISO 7/Grade B, which can drop to Grade C if closed; RABS in ISO 8/Grade C, but with no environmental monitoring needed
options.B: Both in ISO 7/Grade B, with identical background requirements regardless of type
options.C: Isolator in ISO 8/Grade C (or a Grade D that achieves ISO 8); RABS usually in ISO 7/Grade B
options.D: Isolator must be in ISO 5/Grade A with no exceptions; RABS in ISO 7/Grade B or lower

questions.explanation: The globally usable isolator background recommendation is ISO 8/Grade C, or a Grade D that reaches ISO 8 both in operation and at rest; a RABS needs the outside to be an aseptic processing environment, usually ISO 7/Grade B. For this reason the amount of environmental monitoring for an isolator is usually significantly less than for a RABS.

questions.question: Since physical glove tests (pressure decay or constant pressure) can already measure glove leaks, why does the document still recommend frequent visual inspection?

options.A: Because visual inspection can replace physical testing, so physical testing can be omitted and done only at annual maintenance
options.B: Because physical tests cannot detect holes of a few micrometers, while trained operators visually inspecting white gloves can find them with high accuracy
options.C: Because visual inspection can quantify the leak rate and be used directly to calculate microbial ingress and risk
options.D: Because physical tests can be done only after the enclosure is closed and decontaminated, so they have no practical use

questions.explanation: Gloves are the weakest part of the system and can leak. Physical testing is usually done with the door open, before decontamination (pressure decay or constant pressure), but cannot detect holes of a few micrometers, so microbial contamination cannot be fully excluded; studies show trained staff visually inspecting white gloves can achieve high accuracy, so gloves should be visually inspected daily and physically tested periodically. Visual inspection supplements physical testing and does not replace it.

questions.question: An isolator's H2O2 decontamination cycle failed, and the investigation found that cleaning before decontamination was incomplete. Why does incomplete cleaning cause this result?

options.A: Residues block hydrogen peroxide from reaching the surfaces, causing the decontamination cycle to fail, so thorough cleaning must come first
options.B: Detergent residues make hydrogen peroxide decompose immediately into water and oxygen, so the cycle time is shortened and decontamination is more thorough
options.C: Incomplete cleaning affects only appearance and has no effect on the 6-log biodecontamination effect
options.D: H2O2 decontamination can replace cleaning, so mechanical cleaning and drying before decontamination are not needed, only a longer exposure time

questions.explanation: The document states that critical surfaces must be effectively cleaned before biodecontamination; failed or incomplete cleaning prevents hydrogen peroxide from reaching the surfaces and causes the decontamination cycle to fail. Before decontamination the isolator should be mechanically cleaned (and dried if the decontaminant requires), with cleaning validation showing the cleaning is effective; decontamination effectiveness is usually shown with BIs (Geobacillus stearothermophilus) to achieve 6-log.

questions.question: Which statement about leak rate testing of an isolator enclosure is consistent with the document?
